description_full: Interpump Group S.p.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacturing and selling of high-pressure pumps in Italy, rest of Europe, North America, the Far East and the Pacific Area, and internationally. The company is involved in the design and distribution of volumetric pumps; production, sale, and distribution of pressure systems and pumps; production of mechanical sifters; production and sale of equipment for the food processing, chemicals, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals industries; galvanic treatment of metals; and sale of centrifugal separators. It also engages in drawing, shearing, and pressing sheet metal; design, production, and sale of mechanized milking systems; production and sale of power take-offs, hydraulic pumps, hydraulic cylinders, valves, rotary unions, hydraulic hoses, and fittings, as well as rubber mixtures, rigid and flexible hydraulic lines, and directional controls; sale of ancillary products for industrial vehicles; surface treatments; and smelting of ferrous metals, cast iron, and aluminum. In addition, the company is involved in the production and sale of power transmission systems, planetary gears, ratiomotors, and drive wheels; and the design, production, and sale of piping systems. Further, it offers water-jetting and hydraulics-related components, as well as flanges, oil tanks, gears, orbital motors, steering system, cylinder, mixers, plunger pumps, special pumps, cleaning systems, and valves and tanks. Interpump Group S.p.A. was founded in 1977 and is based in Sant'ilario D'enza, Italy.

financial_summary: Interpump Group S.p.a. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $5.4B market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 7% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $259M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.60× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.1×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 27% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
